turns.t: Doctor, I've come for the glaucoma check. The pressure test. I'm not sure when I'm meant to be here, I think it's every six months.
That's right. Let me look at your notes. You've been on drops since your diagnosis. Remind me, what are you using?
One drop, in each eye, at night. It's called latanoprost.
Good. Do you ever miss it? ~
Sometimes, if I fall asleep early. Maybe once a week. ~
How are your eyes? Any change in your vision?
I think my side vision is a bit narrower. I bumped into a door the other day.
When did you first notice that?
Oh, a few months ago? Perhaps longer. I honestly can't say.
Any eye pain, redness, or haloes around lights?
No pain. No redness. No haloes.
Any headaches?
No, none.
Any other conditions?
High blood pressure, and short-sightedness.
Right. Let's do the tests. First the pressure. Put your chin on the rest. ~
Okay.
The pressure in your right eye is 17 and the left is 19, which is within normal range on treatment.
Is that good? ~
Yes, that's in the target range. Now I'll look at the back of the eye, with the drops to enlarge your pupils. ~
Will it blur things? ~
A bit, for a few hours. Don't drive.
The optic nerves look a little more cupped on the left than last time, and your visual field test shows a slight loss at the edges, a bit more than before.
Is it getting worse? ~
There's been a small change in the left eye. I'd say your glaucoma is progressing slowly in that eye, even though the pressure is controlled.
Oh dear. ~
It's a gradual condition. The aim is to slow it down. I'd like you to take the drops every night without fail.
I will. I'll put them by my toothbrush. ~
And I'd like to arrange a repeat visual field test and a scan of the optic nerve in three months.
Three months. Okay. ~
Please don't drive until the dilating drops have worn off.
My daughter's driving me home. ~
Good. Thank you for coming. ~
Thank you, doctor. ~
